chief_complaint: fiery red plaque on face with sharply demarcated raised border
hpi_details: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with fiery red plaque on face with sharply demarcated raised border. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he is having a violent allergic reaction to a new facial cleanser or shaving cream he used recently.
concerns: He is worried that this bright red rash will leave permanent scars on his face before his upcoming wedding next month.
expectations: He hopes to receive an allergy injection or a fast-acting soothing cream to calm the facial swelling immediately.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Erysipelas (facial) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Erysipelas facial: IV Penicillin G or Cefazolin, monitor closely, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: fiery red plaque on face with sharply demarcated raised border

Key HPI features: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with fiery red plaque on face with sharply demarcated raised border. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.3C, HR 96, BP 122/78. Bright red, edematous plaque over the left cheek with a sharply demarcated, raised, indurated border; warm and tender to touch. No orbital involvement, extraocular movements intact.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Erysipelas (facial).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cellulitis (less sharply demarcated) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapid spread, high fever, or signs of sepsis.
management_principles: Assess severity and orbital involvement; treat uncomplicated, nonpurulent facial erysipelas with an oral agent active against Group A Streptococcus (e.g., Penicillin VK or Amoxicillin).
Reserve IV Penicillin G or Cefazolin and admission for systemic toxicity, rapid progression, or inability to tolerate oral therapy.
Outline the borders of the plaque to monitor spread and reassess within 48 hours; escalate urgently for eye symptoms or signs of deeper facial infection.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 29M with a fiery-red, sharply demarcated, raised facial plaque, gradually worsening, with associated fatigue, consistent with a superficial dermal lymphatic infection (Group A Strep).
reference_soap.objective: T 38.3C, HR 96, BP 122/78. Bright red, edematous plaque over the left cheek with a sharply demarcated, raised, indurated border; warm and tender. No orbital involvement, extraocular movements intact.
reference_soap.assessment: Erysipelas of the face, uncomplicated, no orbital or systemic involvement.
reference_soap.plan: Assess severity, systemic toxicity, orbital involvement, and ability to take oral medication. Treat uncomplicated, nonpurulent erysipelas with an oral agent active against streptococci when appropriate; reserve IV penicillin/cefazolin and admission for systemic illness, rapid progression, inability to take oral therapy, or other high-risk features. Escalate urgently for eye symptoms or signs of deeper facial infection.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Erysipelas facial
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Erysipelas facial
Implement evidence-based management plan: IV Penicillin G or Cefazolin, monitor closely

teaching.one_liner: A superficial dermal and lymphatic infection, typically Group A Streptococcus, causing a fiery-red, sharply demarcated, raised plaque, often on the face.
red_flags: Rapid spread, high fever, or signs of sepsis

must_ask.say: Does the redness have a sharp, raised edge?
How quickly did this appear and spread?
Is the area painful and warm to touch?
Any recent cut, insect bite, or skin break on your face?

history.answer: My left cheek suddenly turned fiery red and swollen two days ago, and it's been getting more painful and spreading.
It started about two days ago as a small red spot on my left cheek and has gradually expanded across the cheek over the last 24 hours.
It is only on the left side of my face and cheek, nowhere else on my body.
It is a bright, fiery red raised patch with a very distinct, sharp border that you can easily feel.
It feels burning hot and throbs with pain, especially when touched. It does not itch at all.
I did get a small nick while shaving my left cheek three days ago, right where the redness began.
No, it hasn't faded or come and gone. It has stayed red and swollen continuously and grown larger.
No, I have never had any skin problem or infection like this before.
Yes, I developed chills and a fever yesterday, and I feel completely worn out and fatigued.
No sores in my mouth, no redness or pain in my eye, and my vision is completely normal.
No, the skin is intact without any peeling, blisters, or dark purple spots.
My left cheek is swollen, but my lips and tongue are fine, and I have no trouble breathing, swallowing, or dizziness.
No, I have not started any new prescription drugs, antibiotics, or pain relievers recently.
No new soaps, cosmetics, skincare products, detergents, foods, metals, or plants.
No one at home or work has had a skin rash, fever, or any similar illness.
No bug or tick bites, and I haven't traveled, hiked outdoors, or visited any public baths or saunas.
No, I have never had atopic eczema, asthma, or allergic rhinitis.
No, my joints feel fine and my nails look completely normal.
I have not applied any steroid or antifungal creams, only held a cool damp washcloth on it, which didn't help.
I have one regular sexual partner, no new partners, and no genital ulcers or sores.
I searched my symptoms online and saw pictures of erysipelas, so I was wondering if it could be that.
I'm really worried that this terrible redness will leave permanent scars all over my face right before my wedding next month.
I'm hoping to get an allergy shot or a strong soothing cream to bring the redness and swelling down right away.
I have no chronic medical conditions and have always been healthy.
I have never had any surgery or stayed in a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or nutritional supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications or foods.
I am a non-smoker and have never smoked.
I drink socially, maybe one or two beers on weekends.
I work in an office as an IT specialist and live by myself in an apartment.
My parents and siblings are all healthy, with no family history of skin infections or immune problems.

exam.finding: Patient is alert and oriented, appears mildly fatigued and flushed, with visible left facial swelling and discomfort, but in no acute respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, heart rate 96/min, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 38.3 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.

Fiery bright red, edematous plaque over the left cheek measuring approximately 6x5 cm, with a sharply demarcated, indurated, raised border; warm and tender to touch without fluctuance, bullae, or crepitus; remainder of skin normal.
Extraocular movements fully intact bilaterally without pain or diplopia; pupils equal, round, and reactive to light; no periorbital edema, erythema, proptosis, or conjunctival injection.
Oral mucosa pink and moist without lesions, ulcers, or tonsillar exudates; uvula midline; no lips, tongue, or soft palate swelling.
Palpable, tender left anterior cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy; no contralateral or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Regular rhythm with mild tachycardia; normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation; no wheezing, rhonchi, or crackles.
